title: Server error (5xx)
description: The server failed while answering these URLs. Search engines drop pages that return 5xx repeatedly, and visitors see nothing at all.
howToFix: Check the server's error log for the exact failure. A 500 is usually an application exception, a 502 or 504 an upstream or timeout problem, and a 503 either genuine overload or a maintenance page left switched on. Fix the cause, then re-crawl to confirm. If a 503 is deliberate, send a `Retry-After` header so crawlers come back rather than dropping the page.

title: Client error (4xx)
description: These URLs do not exist or refuse access. Any link, sitemap entry or bookmark pointing at them is wasted, and the link equity they would have passed on is lost.
howToFix: For each URL decide which it is: content that moved, in which case 301 it to the new location; content that is gone for good, in which case leave the 404 and remove the links to it; or a mistake, in which case fix the URL. Do not blanket-redirect everything to the home page — a soft 404 is worse than an honest one. Check the Inlinks panel to find the pages that need editing.

title: URL could not be fetched
description: The request never completed: DNS did not resolve, the connection was refused or reset, TLS failed, or the server did not answer in time. A crawler that cannot reach a page cannot index it.
howToFix: Look at the error type on each row. DNS failures mean a hostname that no longer exists — usually an old subdomain still linked somewhere. Connection failures point at a firewall, a rate limiter reacting to the crawl, or a service that is down. Timeouts mean the page is too slow to render; raise the timeout to confirm, then fix the page. TLS errors mean an expired, mismatched or incomplete certificate chain.

title: Page links to a broken URL
description: These pages contain links to URLs that return 4xx or 5xx. Unlike the error itself, this issue lists the pages you need to edit.
howToFix: Edit each page listed and either correct the link, point it at the replacement content, or remove it. The detail column names one broken target per page; open the page's Outlinks panel to see them all. Fixing links at the source is better than adding a redirect for every typo, because a redirect still costs a round trip on every visit.

title: Redirect loop
description: These URLs redirect in a circle, so nothing is ever served. Browsers show an error after a few hops and search engines give up on the URL entirely.
howToFix: Find the two or more rules that point at each other — commonly an HTTP→HTTPS rule fighting a trailing-slash rule, or a CMS redirect duplicating a server one. Order your rules so each URL is rewritten at most once, and prefer one canonical form (scheme, host, trailing slash) applied in a single place.

title: Canonical points at a broken URL
description: The canonical tag names a URL that does not return 200. A canonical pointing at a 404 or a redirect tells search engines to index something that is not there, which usually means neither URL gets indexed.
howToFix: Point the canonical at the final, working URL — the one that returns 200 directly, with no redirect. Check the scheme, the host and the trailing slash: a canonical to the http:// version of an https:// page is the most common form of this mistake.

title: Mixed content on an HTTPS page
description: These HTTPS pages reference images, stylesheets or scripts over plain HTTP. Browsers block active mixed content outright and warn about passive mixed content, so the page is both broken and insecure.
howToFix: Change every http:// reference on the page to https://, or make it protocol-relative by starting it at the path. Most cases come from hard-coded absolute URLs in old content or in a theme. Once the references are fixed, add a `Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests` header so any that are missed are upgraded rather than blocked.

title: Redirect chain
description: These URLs take more than 2 hops to reach their destination. Every hop adds latency for visitors, and long chains risk being abandoned by crawlers before the destination is reached.
howToFix: Collapse the chain: change each redirect to point straight at the final destination instead of at the next hop. Then update the internal links, the sitemap and any canonical tags to name the destination directly, so the redirect only ever serves external traffic and old bookmarks.

title: Internal link to a redirect
description: These pages link to URLs that redirect. The link works, but every visitor and crawler pays for an extra round trip, and some of the link's value is diluted on the way.
howToFix: Edit the links to point at the destination URL directly. The detail column names the redirecting target; the destination is on that URL's row. This is one of the cheapest wins on most sites, because a site-wide template link to an old URL can account for thousands of wasted requests.

title: Missing title
description: These indexable pages have no `<title>`, or an empty one. The title is the single strongest on-page signal and the headline of every search result, so a missing one costs both ranking and clicks.
howToFix: Write a unique title for each page: the page's subject first, the site name last, between 30 and 60 characters. Describe what the page is, do not stuff keywords, and never reuse the same title across pages.

title: Duplicate title
description: Several indexable pages share the same title. Search engines use it to tell pages apart, so duplicates suggest the pages are interchangeable — and make the ones that do get indexed compete with each other.
howToFix: Give each page a title that describes what is unique about it. Templated titles are the usual cause: a paginated series needs the page number, a filtered listing needs the filter, and a product variant needs the variant. If two pages genuinely are the same, consolidate them and canonicalise one to the other instead.

title: Title too long
description: These titles are longer than 60 characters, so search engines will usually truncate them. Anything past the cut is invisible in the result.
howToFix: Put the important words first and trim the rest. Dropping the site name, or shortening it to an abbreviation, is often enough. The 60-character guide is a proxy for the real limit, which is pixel width, so a title full of capitals or wide letters may be cut sooner.

title: Title too short
description: These titles are shorter than 30 characters. Short is not wrong, but it usually means the page is leaving room unused and describing itself less well than it could.
howToFix: Add the detail a searcher would be looking for: what kind of thing the page is, who it is for, or where it applies. Keep it readable — a title padded out with keywords performs worse than a short, honest one.

title: Missing meta description
description: These indexable pages have no meta description. Search engines then write their own snippet from the page text, which is rarely the pitch you would have chosen.
howToFix: Write 70–155 characters per page saying what the page offers and why to click. It is not a ranking factor, so write it for the reader, not for a keyword. Leave it off deliberately only where the page text genuinely makes a better snippet than anything you would write.

title: Duplicate meta description
description: Several indexable pages share the same meta description. A snippet that describes a whole section rather than the page tends to be discarded and rewritten.
howToFix: Rewrite each one around what that page specifically offers. As with titles, templates are the usual cause; if writing one per page is impractical for thousands of pages, build the description from the page's own fields rather than repeating a constant.

title: Meta description too long
description: These descriptions are longer than 155 characters and will usually be truncated mid-sentence in the search result.
howToFix: Lead with the point. Make the first sentence work on its own, so the description still reads as a complete thought when the rest is cut.

title: Meta description too short
description: These descriptions are shorter than 70 characters, which usually means the snippet says less than it could.
howToFix: Add what the page actually contains or offers. A description of a few words is often a leftover from a template field that was never filled in properly.

title: Missing H1
description: These indexable pages have no `<h1>`. The first heading tells both readers and search engines what the page is about, and screen-reader users rely on it to orient themselves.
howToFix: Add one `<h1>` naming the page's subject. It should agree with the title but need not be identical — the title is written for a search result, the H1 for someone already on the page. If the design has no visible heading, the page probably still needs one; style it rather than removing it.

title: Multiple H1s
description: These pages have more than one `<h1>`. HTML5 permits it, but in practice several top-level headings usually mean the heading hierarchy is being used for styling rather than structure.
howToFix: Keep one `<h1>` for the page's subject and demote the others to `<h2>` or `<h3>` according to how they nest. Check templates first: a header logo wrapped in an `<h1>` plus a page title in another is the most common cause.

title: Missing canonical
description: These indexable pages declare no canonical URL. It is not required, but without one any URL variant that reaches the page — a tracking parameter, a trailing slash, an uppercase path — can be indexed as a separate page.
howToFix: Add a self-referencing `<link rel="canonical" href="…">` with the page's absolute, preferred URL. Most CMSs and frameworks can do this for every page from one template change.

title: Canonicalised to another URL
description: These pages name a different URL as canonical, so they are asking not to be indexed themselves. That is often correct — but it is worth checking that each one is deliberate, because a canonical pointing at the wrong page removes it from search results entirely.
howToFix: Confirm the target is the page you want indexed, that it returns 200, and that its content really is equivalent. A canonical across genuinely different pages is ignored at best and loses you the page at worst. Pagination and filtered listings should usually self-canonicalise instead.

title: Noindex page
description: These pages tell search engines not to index them, via a meta robots tag or an X-Robots-Tag header. Listed so you can check that each one is intended — a `noindex` left on by accident is one of the few SEO mistakes that removes a page completely.
howToFix: Keep `noindex` on pages that genuinely should not appear in search: internal search results, thank-you pages, staging content. Remove it anywhere else. Note that a `noindex` page still consumes crawl budget, so for large sets of them consider blocking the pattern in robots.txt once they are out of the index.

title: Noindex page receives internal links
description: These pages are marked `noindex` but are linked to from elsewhere on the site. The links spend crawl budget and pass value into a page that can never rank.
howToFix: Decide which is wrong. If the page should rank, remove the `noindex`. If it should not, reduce how prominently it is linked — particularly from site-wide navigation — so crawl budget goes to pages that can earn traffic. Do not add `nofollow` to the links: that discards the value rather than redirecting it.

title: Blocked by robots.txt but linked internally
description: robots.txt forbids crawling these URLs, yet the site links to them. A blocked URL can still be indexed from its links, with no content and no description, which is the worst of both outcomes.
howToFix: If the page should be private, use `noindex` — or real access control — rather than robots.txt, and remove the internal links. robots.txt stops crawling, not indexing. If the page should be public, unblock the path in robots.txt so it can be crawled properly.

title: Hreflang missing a return link
description: These pages declare an hreflang alternate that does not point back at them. Hreflang must be reciprocal: an unconfirmed annotation is ignored, so the whole cluster stops working.
howToFix: Every page in a language group must list every page in that group, including itself. If A declares B, then B must declare A. Generate the block from one shared mapping rather than writing it per page, and remember to include the self-referencing entry and an `x-default` where you have one.

title: Hreflang block has no self-reference
description: These pages list hreflang alternates but do not include themselves. A page must name its own language in its own block, or search engines cannot tell which language the page they are looking at is written in, and may discard the whole cluster.
howToFix: Add an entry for the page itself, with its own language code and its own URL. The simplest way to get this right is to generate the block from one list of every URL in the language group and output the same list on every page in it, including the page doing the output.

title: Invalid hreflang language code
description: These hreflang values are not valid language or language-region codes. An unrecognised code is ignored, so the page is left out of its language group.
howToFix: Use an ISO 639-1 language code, optionally followed by a hyphen and an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 *region* code: `en`, `en-GB`, `pt-BR`. The region is a country, not a language — `en-UK` is wrong (the country code is `GB`), and `en_us` uses the wrong separator and case. The only non-language value permitted is `x-default`.

title: Duplicate content
description: These pages have identical text. Search engines pick one and discard the rest, and the choice is theirs, not yours.
howToFix: Consolidate: keep the best version, 301 the others to it, or canonicalise them to it if they must stay reachable. Where duplication is structural — a printer-friendly copy, the same product under two categories — a canonical to the primary URL is the right fix. Where it is thin templated text, write real content or remove the pages.

title: Near-duplicate content
description: These pages are not identical but are more than 91% similar — typically the same text with a different heading, price or date. Search engines treat them as competing versions of one page.
howToFix: Decide whether the differences matter to a reader. If they do, make them substantial: different openings, different detail, different examples. If they do not, consolidate the pages as you would for exact duplicates. Thin pages generated per location or per variant are the usual source.

title: Image missing alt text
description: These pages contain images with no `alt` attribute. Screen-reader users get the file name read out instead of a description, and the image cannot be understood by image search.
howToFix: Describe what the image shows, in a few words, as you would to someone who cannot see it. Purely decorative images should have an empty `alt=""`, which is explicitly different from having none: it tells a screen reader to skip the image rather than announce it.

title: Orphan page
description: Nothing on the site links to these pages. They were found only through the sitemap or a canonical tag. A page with no internal links is hard for crawlers to find and gets almost no internal link value.
howToFix: Link to each page from somewhere relevant — a section index, a related-content block, the navigation if it deserves it. If the page should not be reachable, remove it from the sitemap too, because a sitemap entry with no links is a contradictory signal.

title: HTTP URL on an HTTPS site
description: The site is served over HTTPS, but these internal URLs were crawled over plain HTTP. Even when they redirect, they leak the request to the network and cost an extra round trip.
howToFix: Update the internal links to use https:// directly. Keep a site-wide HTTP→HTTPS redirect for outside traffic, and add an HSTS header (`Strict-Transport-Security`) so browsers stop trying HTTP at all after their first visit.

title: Link with no accessible name
description: These pages contain links a screen reader announces as just "link". An icon-only link with no label, or one wrapping an image with empty alt text, is unusable without sight — and search engines get nothing from it either.
howToFix: Give the link text. If it must look like an icon alone, put the words in `aria-label`, or give the image inside it real alt text describing *the destination* rather than the picture: a home icon's alt is "Home", not "house". WCAG 2.4.4 and 4.1.2.

title: Button with no accessible name
description: A button with no text, label or value is announced as "button" and nothing more, so nobody using a screen reader can know what it does before pressing it.
howToFix: Put text in the button. Where the design is an icon only, add `aria-label` saying what the button *does* — "Close dialog", "Add to basket" — and keep the icon decorative. WCAG 4.1.2.

title: Form field with no label
description: These form fields have no `<label>`, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`. A screen reader reaches the field and can say only "edit text", which makes the form impossible to complete.
howToFix: Add a `<label for="…">` matching the field's id, or wrap the field in the label. A `placeholder` is not a label: it vanishes as soon as someone types, and several screen readers ignore it. Where the design has no room for visible text, `aria-label` is the right answer. WCAG 1.3.1 and 3.3.2.

title: ARIA reference points at nothing
description: An `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` on these pages names an element id that is not on the page. The reference is silently dropped, so the element ends up with no name at all — worse than if the attribute had never been added.
howToFix: Check each id actually exists and is spelled identically; they are case-sensitive. This usually follows a template change that renamed or removed the element being pointed at. Watch for ids that only exist after JavaScript runs, which is too late for some assistive technology.

title: Page does not declare a language
description: These pages have no `lang` attribute on `<html>`. A screen reader then guesses, and reads English in a French accent or the reverse — which ranges from irritating to incomprehensible.
howToFix: Add `lang` to the `<html>` element: `<html lang="en-GB">`. Mark any passage in another language with its own `lang` too. This is one attribute, it takes a minute, and it is WCAG 3.1.1 at level A.

title: Duplicate element id
description: The same `id` appears more than once on these pages. Every `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby` and `<label for>` pointing at it resolves to the first one only, so some controls quietly get the wrong name or none.
howToFix: Make each id unique. Duplicates almost always come from a component rendered several times with a hard-coded id — generate one per instance instead. WCAG 4.1.1.

title: Invalid ARIA role
description: These pages use a `role` that ARIA does not define. An unrecognised role is ignored outright, so the element falls back to its native semantics — or, on a `<div>`, to none at all.
howToFix: Correct the spelling against the ARIA role list. The usual culprits are invented names like `role="clickable"` and near-misses like `role="buton"`. Better still, use the element that already has the semantics: a `<button>` needs no role.

title: Positive tabindex
description: A `tabindex` greater than zero pulls an element to the front of the tab order, ahead of everything in document order. One of them rearranges keyboard navigation for the whole page, usually in a way nobody intended.
howToFix: Use `tabindex="0"` to make something focusable in its natural position, or `-1` for something only script will focus. If the tab order is wrong, fix the order of the markup rather than overriding it. WCAG 2.4.3.

title: Frame with no title
description: An `<iframe>` with no `title` is announced as just "frame". Someone navigating by frame has no way to tell the video from the map from the advert.
howToFix: Add `title` describing what the frame contains — "Office location map", not "iframe". A frame that is purely decorative or offscreen should carry `aria-hidden="true"` instead. WCAG 4.1.2.

title: Heading level skipped
description: These pages jump down more than one heading level at once, such as an `<h2>` straight to an `<h4>`. Screen-reader users navigate by heading, and a gap reads as a missing section.
howToFix: Use heading levels to describe structure, not size: go down one level at a time and style them with CSS. Jumping back *up* any number of levels is fine — that is just a new section. WCAG 1.3.1.

title: Slow response
description: These URLs took longer than 1000 ms to respond. Server response time is the floor under every other speed metric: nothing on the page can start until the first byte arrives.
howToFix: Look for the usual culprits: an uncached database query per request, a slow third-party call made during rendering, or no page cache at all. Measure where the time goes before optimising. Note that this is server time only, measured from a local crawl — it is not a Core Web Vitals score, which Phase 5's PageSpeed integration will provide.

title: Oversized image
description: These images are larger than 100 KB. Images are usually the heaviest part of a page, and an oversized one delays everything that follows it.
howToFix: Serve WebP or AVIF instead of JPEG or PNG, resize to the dimensions actually displayed rather than relying on the browser to scale down, and use `srcset` so small screens get small files. Add `loading="lazy"` to images below the fold — but never to the main image at the top of the page, which should load as early as possible.

title: Page buried deep in the site
description: These pages are more than 5 clicks from the start URL. Depth is a reasonable proxy for how important a site treats a page: the deeper it is, the less often it is crawled and the less internal link value it receives.
howToFix: Shorten the path to the pages that matter. Add section hubs, link related content across sections, and keep pagination short — a 40-page paginated archive buries everything past page two. Check the crawl-depth distribution in the report: a site whose pages cluster at depth six or more usually has a navigation problem, not a content one.
